chapters.title: Commodity Markets in India — Structure and Players

lessons.title: What Are Commodity Derivatives and Why They Exist

children.text: On 28 April 2022, Indonesia banned all exports of palm oil overnight. India imports more edible oil than any other country in the world, and palm oil is typically the single largest component of that basket. A refiner in Kandla who had already quoted prices to biscuit makers and hotel chains for the next two months suddenly faced a raw material bill that could jump 20% or more, with no way to go back and renegotiate contracts he had already signed. Indonesia lifted the ban three weeks later, on 23 May 2022, but for that stretch, every edible oil business in India was staring at the same question: how do you protect a business from a price move you cannot predict and cannot control? Commodity derivatives exist to answer exactly that question.

body.text: A commodity derivative is a contract whose value is derived from the price of an underlying commodity, agreed today for a transaction that settles later. It lets two parties fix a price in advance without either of them needing to hold, store or move the physical commodity today.

children.text: From Bombay Cotton to MCX and NCDEX

This is not a new problem, and India was not late to solve it. Cotton traders in Bombay were fixing forward prices before the British Raj had electric light in most of the city. What has changed since then is the plumbing: who regulates the contracts, who guarantees them, and how easily an ordinary investor can access them.

body.title: Commodity derivatives in India: a short history

events.title: The Bombay Cotton Trade Association
events.description: Cotton merchants in Bombay organise futures trading in cotton, making it one of the oldest organised futures markets in Asia.

events.title: The Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act
events.description: The government sets up the Forward Markets Commission (FMC) to regulate commodity forward and futures trading, and restricts or bans futures in several commodities over the following decades on inflation-control grounds.

events.title: MCX and NCDEX are launched
events.description: The Multi Commodity Exchange (MCX) and the National Commodity and Derivatives Exchange (NCDEX) both begin operations within weeks of each other, bringing electronic, nationwide futures trading to commodities for the first time.

events.title: FMC merges into SEBI
events.description: The Forward Markets Commission is merged into the Securities and Exchange Board of India. One regulator now oversees both equity derivatives and commodity derivatives, closing the gap that had let commodity market oversight lag behind.

body.text: Notice what did not change across 150 years: the underlying need. A cotton merchant in 1875 and an edible oil refiner in 2022 were solving the identical problem, fixing a price today for a transaction that happens later. What changed is who guarantees the other side keeps their word, which is exactly the gap an exchange and its clearing corporation fill. You will see this in detail in the next lesson.

children.text: Every commodity derivative derives its value from an
commodity, but there is more than one way to structure that contract. The simplest version, a

, is a private, customised agreement between two parties, say a turmeric exporter and a spice processor, to trade at an agreed price on an agreed future date. It is flexible on quantity and delivery terms, but it carries

, because nobody guarantees either side actually shows up. A futures contract solves that by standardising everything except price and putting an exchange's clearing corporation in the middle as guarantor to both sides. An options contract goes a step further, giving the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to trade at a fixed price, in exchange for an upfront premium.

body.title: Forward or futures?
body.question: A sugar mill and a soft drink company privately agree that the mill will sell the company 500 tonnes of sugar at ₹38,000 per tonne, six months from now, with delivery at the company's factory gate. Neither party is a member of any exchange. What is this?
options: A futures contract, because a price and date are fixed
A forward contract, because it is a private, customised deal with no exchange involved
An options contract, because both sides have flexibility
Not a derivative at all, since no exchange is involved
body.explanation: It is a forward contract: two parties negotiating a customised deal directly, bearing each other's counterparty risk, with no exchange or clearing corporation involved. It is still a derivative, since its value derives from the future price of sugar.

children.text: Why Derivatives Exist: Four Jobs They Do
A futures exchange only works because different people show up wanting different things. Four roles matter, and this course will keep coming back to all four.

body.caption: The four jobs a commodity futures market does
headers: What they are trying to do

cells: Transfer price risk they are already exposed to, in exchange for giving up some potential upside
A Rajkot gold jeweller sells gold futures to lock in today's price for jewellery he will deliver next month
Arrive at a transparent, continuously updated price that reflects all available information
Bullion dealers across India quote physical gold rates off the live MCX gold price
Speculators: traders with no underlying business exposure
Take on price risk deliberately, betting on direction, to try and profit
A retail trader on Zerodha's Kite goes long on MCX crude oil, expecting prices to rise
Profit from small, temporary price gaps for the same or a related asset across markets
A trader buys gold on MCX and simultaneously sells it on COMEX when the two prices, adjusted for the rupee and import duty, drift out of line

body.text: Do not think of speculators as the villains of this story. A hedger who wants to sell risk needs someone willing to buy it. If every single participant in a market were a hedger trying to offload risk, there would be nobody left to take the other side of the trade. Speculators supply the liquidity that makes hedging possible in the first place.

body.text: This is leverage, and it cuts both ways. It is also why futures are classified as hedging and speculation instruments rather than plain investments: a small price move against you can wipe out a large share of your margin. Chapter 2 covers margins and mark-to-market in full.

body.title: Name the role
body.scenario: Three people place orders on MCX crude oil futures on the same morning. Ramesh runs a fleet of diesel-guzzling trucks and buys crude futures to protect his business against a price spike he cannot pass on to customers immediately. Ananya has never touched diesel or crude in her life; she reads a geopolitical news report and buys crude futures purely because she expects prices to rise this week. Vikram notices that MCX crude is trading slightly cheap relative to its international benchmark once you adjust for the rupee, and buys MCX crude while simultaneously selling a matching position abroad to lock in the gap.
body.prompt: For each of Ramesh, Ananya and Vikram, name the role they are playing in this market and explain what each is actually trying to achieve.
body.modelAnswer:
Ramesh is a hedger. He already carries real diesel price risk through his trucking business, and he uses futures to offset that risk rather than to create a new bet.
Ananya is a speculator. She has no underlying business exposure to crude oil; she is deliberately taking on price risk in the hope of a profit, based on her view of the news.
Vikram is an arbitrageur. He is not betting on the direction of crude prices at all. He is exploiting a temporary price gap between two markets and expects to profit regardless of which way crude moves next, as long as the gap closes.

body.label: Why "the MCX price" matters beyond the exchange
body.value: It becomes the reference price for physical trade
body.context: Bullion dealers, refiners and processors across India price real, physical transactions off the exchange futures price, even when neither party ever intends to trade on the exchange itself. That is price discovery at work.

The actual commodity whose price a derivative contract's value depends on.
A private, customised agreement between two parties to trade at a fixed price on a future date, carrying counterparty risk.
A standardised, exchange-traded version of a forward, guaranteed by a clearing corporation.
The risk that the other party to a contract fails to honour it.
A market participant with real underlying exposure who uses derivatives to reduce price risk.
A participant with no underlying exposure who takes on price risk deliberately, aiming to profit from price moves.

The process by which a market's continuous trading arrives at a transparent price reflecting all available information.

points: A commodity derivative derives its value from an underlying commodity's price and lets two parties fix a price today for a transaction that settles later.

India's organised futures markets date back to 1875 with the Bombay Cotton Trade Association, one of Asia's oldest. MCX and NCDEX, launched in 2003, brought electronic nationwide trading, and SEBI has regulated commodity derivatives since the FMC merged into it on 28 September 2015.

Forwards are private and customised but carry counterparty risk. Futures standardise the contract and remove that risk through a clearing corporation. Options add the right, but not the obligation, to trade, for a premium.

Markets need four roles to function: hedgers transfer risk, speculators take it on for profit and supply liquidity, arbitrageurs keep prices consistent across markets, and the whole process delivers price discovery that even non-traders rely on.
Futures require only a fraction of the contract value as margin, which magnifies both gains and losses. This leverage is central to why derivatives suit hedging and speculation, not casual investing.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Commodity futures and options are leveraged instruments and can result in losses larger than your initial margin. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before trading.
